h: The curator who collected friends as well as art
p: Jim Ede wasn't just a collector with deep pockets. In the 1920s and 30s he worked at the Tate Gallery in London, where he got to know many of the artists whose work you'll see on the walls. Some gave him pictures as gifts, some sold them for very little, and that's how a man of fairly modest means ended up with such a remarkable collection.

Two stories stand out. Henri Gaudier-Brzeska was a brilliant young French sculptor who was killed in the First World War, and Ede acquired a large part of his estate when hardly anyone was interested. Alfred Wallis was a retired Cornish fisherman who only started painting in his seventies, using ship's paint on scraps of cardboard. Ede championed him when many in the art world would have walked straight past. Find their work in the house and those back-stories really add to it.
Allow an hour or two for the house and the gallery together. It's a calm, slow sort of place, so it suits grown-ups and older kids better than toddlers who want to run about.

Castle Street has a couple of other treats close by. The Museum of Cambridge, in an old coaching inn, tells the story of everyday life in the town and surrounding fens. Wander down the hill towards the river and Magdalene College is home to the Pepys Library, where the famous diarist's books are kept. Grab a coffee in this quieter corner of the city before heading into the busier centre.
